utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, may we have the appearances, please. For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Kenneth Scott for the Prosecutor, along with Mr. Roeland Bos and Ms. Marie-Ursula Kind. I do expect Mr. Stringer and Mr. Poriouvaev soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. The lead counsel for the Defence is Mr. Kresimir Krsnik, attorney from Zagreb, co-counsel Christopher Meek and legal assistant Nika Pinter, an attorney from Zagreb. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. I am Branko Seric, counsel for Vinko Martinovic, and next to me is my co-counsel, Mr. Zelimir Par.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Martinovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language you can understand? THE ACCUSED MARTINOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It has been about six weeks since we saw each other. Do you have anything to complain during that period? THE ACCUSED MARTINOVIC: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Mr. Naletilic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand? THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about your health? THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid you have to take care of your health since it's the time for the changing of the season at this moment. THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] I am taking care of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Well, it is a long time, and welcome back to this trial. This is a pre-defence conference held in accordance with Rule 73 ter. The purpose of this conference is to help the Defence counsel to prepare their case. So we are only dealing with the procedural matters rather than the substantive ones. There were several issues that we have to address during this conference. The first one is the Rule 65 ter filings, namely, the total number of witness and the estimated length of their testimony; two, the Rule 71 motion filed by Defence counsel of Naletilic on deposition; thirdly, the Rule 92 bis written statement; four, expert witness the Defence intends to call; fifth, protective measures for the Defence witnesses; sixth, exhibits; seven, the procedural matters concerning the first day of the trial; eighth, other matters. This Trial Chamber issued an order in respect of the pre-defence filings dated March 12th, 2002. In that order, the Trial Chamber requests for both parties to meet and discuss all of the above mentioned matters and to present to the Chamber the results of that meeting, as well as the areas of agreement at this pre-defence conference. Now, first of all, we would like to hear the parties on the meeting, and later on, we will deal with those special matters one by one. Are there anybody from the parties who volunteers to take the floor first? Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, it has been six weeks, but it has been like a brief moment for the Defence, and I really don't know where to begin because there is so much to report and so many problems about which I should tell Your Honours. So I will start with today's meeting with our learned friends. I'm afraid that there are many matters on which we have not reached an agreement. The Defence wanted to reach agreement on two issues, one of which is at least the names of people who, in order to save time, will not have protective measures objected to by the Prosecution. And secondly, I asked my learned friends to agree on the safe passage motion, that is, we would like to avoid having to ask for safe passage for each witness separately. My learned friends have enormous power. By this, I do not mean that they abuse it; quite the contrary. But in view of the fact that they do have a list of witnesses, I thought we could agree which of our witnesses do not need safe passage and which of them might require this. However, we have not managed to reach an agreement on this either because our learned friends have told us that this has to do with the relationship between the Defence counsel and the Court. And we agree with this, but we did try to reach an agreement with them about this. So I would like to inform Your Honours that the Defence will submit requests. We asked for one safe passage to -- for two safe passages today, one -- however, we would like to make a single submission asking for safe passage for all the witnesses because we do not want anything to happen to any of the witnesses arriving here voluntarily. Since we do not know what the intentions of the Prosecution are, we are forced to ask for this so that our case can proceed without any problems and to avoid anything at all happening to any of our witnesses, because then, of course, the Defence would not have any more witnesses to call. No one would want to come. Your Honours, I have good reason for saying this. I spent a number of months in Mostar, and just before I left for The Hague, all the media in Bosnia and Herzegovina published 60 new indictments -- they're speculating. No one knows exactly who is indicted, who is not. Everyone is upset, and this is certainly one of the reasons we are asking for this. The Defence will make this submission, and we ask the Chamber to respond to it. We further discussed depositions with our learned friends and the purpose for depositions. Unfortunately, I have to say that we have not reached agreement on this either. The Defence truly feels that depositions would meet their purpose for several reasons: First, in order to expedite the proceedings; secondly, for reasons of judicial economy; thirdly, because it is not insignificant that they would appear after seven years later; and another reason are the expenses. Of course, it is much cheaper to take depositions in Mostar. We went to the court there. We looked at the premises. The court has been renovated. It has all the facilities needed to -- for us to be able to take depositions without any problems. Furthermore, we would save time and money for the witnesses as well. And also, we would solve a lot of problems concerning safe passage. They live there. The Victims and Witnesses Unit would not have to take care of them. So it would really be much more convenient, for all these reasons. Furthermore, Your Honours, we also discussed the summaries of the witness statements. There are a number of problems here, but I will not go into them now. I am sure Your Honours will ask for further clarification. If Your Honours or our learned friends are not satisfied with the amount of detail and the extent of the summaries, we can provide oral explanations. We can expand on these. But we did not have time. Another problem, and I will ask Your Honours' assistance with this: We are having a lot of problems connected with translation. About 80 per cent of our evidence has not been translated, so I truly do not know how we shall be able to present this evidence. I have informed Mr. Fourmy of all these problems. We have achieved an agreement on certain priorities, so I hope that this problem will be solved on time to avoid any damage to the Defence case. Your Honours, we further discussed a problem which I found in Mostar talking to the president of the court, asking for additional information about their files. We have informed you of this problem in a written submission, and we have discussed it with our learned friends today. It is my duty to inform Your Honours that there are parallel indictments which have been brought before the joint court in Mostar and the cantonal and other courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Defence has come into possession of an indictment, and I will be very explicit now -- against 22 members of the HVO from Sovici. This indictment is dated -- it is dated the 1st of February, 1996. But its number is KT 10/94, which means that it was filed in 1994, two years later. We can only assume what the reason for this is, and we shall have witnesses testify to this, because according to the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina, three months after the completion of an investigation, if an indictment is not issued, then the proceedings are terminated. In any case, we have an indictment against 24 members of the HVO from Sovici, accused of all the crimes with which my client has been charged before this Tribunal. However, neither my client nor the Convicts Battalion are mentioned at all in this indictment. And to make matters even more interesting, the same witnesses are testifying there as the ones who testified here. Although, the president of the high court in Mostar - and he will testify here if need be - has informed me in writing that this file, like all the other files, is in the Prosecutor's office. I don't know whether he was referring to 1997 or 1998. Proceedings have also be brought in the high court in Mostar against the former representative of the Office of the Interior of the HZHB, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. He has been charged under command responsibility for all camps and prisons. And this person has also been accused of the same crimes as my client, in Siroki Brijeg. There is no mention of my client in this file relating to the events in the Siroki Brijeg police station. Unfortunately, we have been unable to get hold of this document. We are searching for it, and I hope we shall have it before our opening statement. And then it will have to be translated. As for this indictment, we are waiting for the translation, and of course, when it is translated, I will submit it to Your Honours and to my learned friends. We have asked our learned friends -- today, we asked them for information about this document, and the answer was that they are still looking for it. If they find it, I hope it will be delivered to us. Your Honours, apart from these parallel indictments, as we can see in the grounds for the indictment and the witness summaries, nowhere -- although the counts are very specific. They mention the mosque, Ljubuski, the school, names of witnesses. These witnesses made statements to the investigating judge. They made statements at the trial. Because we have a decision about a trial in absentia dated the 29th of May, 1996, so this trial was conducted in absentia. And witnesses were examined. A judgement was issued, which I unfortunately do not have. But in any case, the witnesses testified. When the translation of this document has been completed, you will recognise the same witnesses who testified in this courtroom, and it will be very interesting to compare the testimonies with the testimonies they gave in Mostar. Had the Defence had this during its cross-examination, their answers would certainly have been interesting. The Defence feels -- or the Defence believes that they did not mention my client during these trials. Furthermore, Your Honours, let me first explain the situation in the high court in Mostar. In 1999, the court which was active on the east side of Mostar and the court on the west side were joined into a single court, today called the cantonal court. The Croats call it the high court. It is actually the same court. And it is now in a building on the west bank. The president of the court is a Croat, and the cantonal prosecutor is a Bosniak. Cooperation between them is, to put it mildly, as it was before 1995. Communication is limited. Nobody trusts anybody else. When these courts were joined together, the same was done with their archives. The Bosniak side did not put a single case record in the joint archives, and they informed the president of the court in writing that all the case files were in The Hague. After this, the president of the court wrote to the OTP in The Hague, asking at least for copies so that he could complete his archives, but he has not received an answer to date. This brief introduction concerning the court in Mostar has been presented so that I could explain to you what happened to me in Mostar. We asked to inspect the archives of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The minister of justice, whose name is Zvonko Mijan, and who is a Croat, approved this and gave us permission so as to put us on an equal footing with the counsel defending accused who are members of the Bosniak people and who have free access. For this reason, access was also approved for the defence of Mladen Naletilic. I will have this document translated. Then he asked the prime minister to have this implemented under his authority. On the 13th of February, 2000, through the federal Ministry of Justice, the deputy minister, Mr. Ferid Buljubasic informed me as follows: "After consulting the Prosecution of the ICTY and inspecting the documents regulating the operation of this International Tribunal, and the procedure in cases such as this, we received a reply -- " and he's referring to the OTP of this Tribunal -- "that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, IT-92 of the 30th of November, 1999 provides for a procedure regarding information and documents necessary for the preparation of a trial." I will not read the whole letter to you, but they are referring me to the court and telling me to ask for a subpoena. At the same time, the Defence counsel defending Bosniak accused have free access. After this, I applied to the presidency of the Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the moment, this is chaired by a Croat, Joso Krusanovic, and he issued a decision under the title of "Conclusion," ordering his subordinates to give me access to the archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina and giving the same approval to my colleague, Mr. Jonjic, who is the Defence counsel of Pasko Ljubicic before this Tribunal. I have not received a reply to date, and I am convinced that I will never get one. This is only one of the problems I have come across. I think that we shall have ample for you to hear all the evidence. Your Honour, you know the importance of the archives of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially when you hear my opening statement on Monday, which gives a completely different picture from the picture presented by others, for various reasons. History cannot be falsified, nor can it be given different interpretations through indictments. What happened happened, and this is the evidence that will be presented by the Defence, whatever it may be, because Your Honours, the Defence will bring forward witnesses who have never been contacted by anyone so far, anyone at all. And we shall present evidence. However, I will not now embark upon my opening statement. The objectivity of those who are sitting at this trial will be given an opportunity to come to the fore. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seric, do you have anything to add to the statement made by your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have anything to add to what my colleague Mr. Krsnik said. I would like to say, in accordance with the agenda that you have presented, that we have submitted to our colleagues from the OTP and to you, Your Honours, the number of witnesses involved, first of all, with their initials and then with their names and surnames. We have also provided brief summaries of their statements. This number was 38, including Professor Doctor Josip Skavic, who will be an expert witness. So the number would actually be 37. Your Honour, I wanted to say this in line with the agenda, that we were aware of the fact that perhaps this number just sounds bigger than that that you had suggested to us as the right kind of number. However, if you look at the timetable, if you look at the number of days involved, you will see that we will not use up any more time if this number of witnesses were to be 25 or 28, because then these witnesses would involve a longer number of hours that the Defence would need with them. So this number of witnesses, in the view of this Defence, believes that this guarantees that we would use up approximately one working day, as was the case during the Prosecution case, one working day per witness, and perhaps we would be able to deal with even more than one witness per day. So I think that the total we would use would be seven to eight weeks at the most. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honours, I would respond to, I think, two of the more basic points and the ones that the Chamber ordered us or directed the parties to respond to first, and then I will come back to the number of, if I can say miscellaneous items, raised by Mr. Krsnik. I will start with the question about the depositions. First, it is true that we met with Defence counsel today and discussed these matters. I think it's also important to clarify the status of this issue and the position of the respective parties. And by that I mean three parties, not two. And that is, I've confirmed with Mr. Seric and Mr. Par today that the Martinovic Defence does not propose or request any deposition witnesses. So the issues -- I think this is interesting for the Chamber in considering the positions of the Defence of Mr. Naletilic, that apparently these issues, these very same issues, do not rise to the same level of concern with the Defence of Mr. Martinovic. The Prosecution position, Mr. President and Your Honours, on the accused Tuta's proposal to take depositions is not new or surprising. Indeed, this is a topic that has been discussed since last fall. The Prosecution has consistently stated its position, both orally in court and in our various filings since last fall and including in additional filings in January and again more recently. Rule 71, as you know, and this Chamber's prior rulings, require a party to make specific showings in support of requests for depositions. These, in fact, are indeed the same showings that the Prosecution was required to make in proposing depositions in its case, showings that the Prosecution in fact was required to make over Defence objections. The Prosecution since last fall has repeatedly invited the Tuta Defence to make these showings. The Prosecution respectfully submits that up to the present time, including today, the Tuta Defence has provided no sufficient information in support of the required showings. The Trial Chamber itself, in fact, in its order in respect of Defence filings dated the 12th of March, 2002 has ordered the Defence to, and I quote, "file additional information about the witnesses they intend to call." And indeed, as the Chamber knows, the Prosecution shares serious concerns about the adequacy of the filings made by the Defence and particularly by the Tuta Defence in recent weeks. The information is indeed deficient for many purposes, including making the required showings under Rule 71 and this Chamber's prior rulings. I have said to the Defence many times and I have said to them again this morning that if and when and at such time as they present us with sufficient information, we will make further assessments about whether we believe in our view - of course subject to the Chamber's determination - that any of the witnesses are appropriate for deposition. Let me further note the following on this: Directing the Court's attention back to the Trial Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's motion to take depositions -- that decision was dated the 10th of November, 2000, when the -- this Chamber was constituted differently, and involving Judge Wald. Interesting to note -- interesting to note that in that filings, when the Defence was opposing deposition, the Chamber noted in that decision dated the 10th November that the Defence position was that, "The interest of justice in this case requires that all witnesses be heard directly by the fully constituted Trial Chamber." Now, that's interesting because that was this Defence position in November 2000, that all witnesses should be heard by this Trial Chamber, when they objected to Prosecution depositions. The Chamber went on to say, "Finding that the witnesses proposed by the Prosecution are suitable witnesses to give evidence by way of deposition -- " I won't read the entire order but very specifically, made very specific findings on the proper testimony, why it was suitable, et cetera, et cetera, and made specific rulings. The Prosecution position on this has been that the Defence, no different from the Prosecution, has to make the required showings. I would also note a prior decision of this Chamber. It was a decision on the Prosecutor's motion to take additional depositions for use at trial dated the 5th of June, 2001. The Chamber may recall that before the depositions started in July 2001, the Prosecution in fact, based on a continuing assessment of its case, proposed to take additional depositions at that time. This Trial Chamber denied the Prosecution's request because in its view, the Trial Chamber was unable to determine whether the witnesses were repetitive to an acceptable degree of testimony to be given by live witnesses and whether they were so unduly repetitive that allowing them to present evidence by deposition would unreasonably prolong the proceedings. There again, the Chamber -- specific showings were made. The Chamber made specific rulings, and in fact refused the witnesses tendered by the Prosecution for depositions. Thus -- and I summarise here on this point -- thus it is the Prosecution's first basis of opposition to the depositions requested by the Naletilic Defence that no showings have been provided, have been made, and indeed let alone the showings, no appropriate or sufficient information has been provided to the Prosecution to allow us to make any informed judgements about whether any of that evidence would be acceptable for deposition. Second, as a separate matter, the Prosecution is opposed to taking the depositions -- should the Chamber decide that any depositions are appropriate, the Prosecution is opposed to taking the depositions in Mostar or Sarajevo. We submit, Your Honours, that the proposals put forward by the Tuta Defence, if accepted, would involve a substantial shift in Tribunal practice and policy and would create a dangerous and unfair situation, with one set of rules for the Prosecution and another set of rules or practices for the Defence. Under the Defence proposals, the logic of those proposals is this: The Prosecution will always be faced with presenting its witnesses in The Hague either by live testimony or deposition, but deposition if at all in The Hague, with all the issues that that raises, as the Chamber knows - excuse me - with the witness availability and a whole host of other issues. By contrast, the Defence -- not only in this case, but by the exact same logic in all cases, would always be in a more favourable position of take depositions in the field. This would or could create at least two disadvantages to the Prosecution or advantages to the Defence. First of all, witness availability. This Chamber has heard extensive evidence since the trial started about the difficulties with bringing witnesses to The Hague. Nonetheless, the Prosecution did its best to meet its burden and to bring witnesses here. If deposition or taking of testimony was approved in Mostar, the Defence would be given a tremendous advantage in calling witnesses who are not willing or able to come to The Hague. The Prosecution would object to that. Further, it also would affect the issues which we believe are very important, and that is the questions of witness appearance and credibility. Unlike the Prosecution witnesses, the Defence witnesses would not be seen and heard directly by the Trial Chamber. And indeed that goes back to the very language of the Defence itself, noted in the Chamber's prior ruling that it was fundamentally important to justice that all witnesses be seen and heard by the Judges themselves directly. That is the Defence's own words. There is also the danger that taking evidence away from The Hague courtroom lowers the seriousness and the gravity which must attend the taking and giving of evidence. Again, in this Chamber's own decision on the Prosecutor's motion to take depositions dated the 10th of November, 2000, the -- the Chamber at that time noted the accused Martinovic's position. And we have no quarrel with the Martinovic Defence at this time. But nonetheless, the Martinovic's position at that time, and I quote; this is from the Chamber's ruling of the 10th of November, 2000: "Depositions -- " excuse me. "Depositions taken away from the seat of the Tribunal in the preparatory stages of the proceedings are less reliable as the evidence is given in an informal environment, and the witnesses may be subjected to pressure by local authorities." We submit, Your Honour, respectfully, that those issues -- the very issues raised by the Defence, are equally valid now. We also note the issues concerning witnesses. Again, the Chamber well knows, respectfully, that the issues that Mr. Krsnik has raised concerning witnesses are not unique to his -- I shouldn't use that term. The witnesses which the Defence would like to call, as it has been with the witnesses that the Prosecution has called. Why would the Defence witnesses receive more favourable treatment than the Prosecution witnesses? And indeed, I must -- I must indicate to the Chamber, because these proceedings are followed closely in Bosnia, this would affect the Bosnian public's view and impression of the Tribunal. All of the Prosecution witnesses who came to The Hague at considerable hardship, at considerable personal expense, not covered by the types of expenses that the Tribunal pays for, at considerable inconvenience to their families might well ask and might well talk in their communities, "Why did we have to go to The Hague and the Defence witnesses can stay in Mostar?" I submit, respectfully, Your Honours, that would not be a favourable impression to create to the international public or to the people in Bosnia. "Why did we have to go to The Hague and the Defence witnesses can stay in Mostar?" And it would even raise such a question, it would even raise the issue of the location of the depositions even at a very micro level. Indeed, as the Chamber has heard, would they be taken in East Mostar or would they be taken in West Mostar? The issue with expense, Your Honours, we are not convinced that the taking of depositions in Mostar would be substantially financially cheaper than testimony in The Hague and, in fact, the expense may well be greater. It may well be greater. Substantial measures have to be put in place and staff made available in the field, including a hearing officer, a court clerk, a registry representative, court reporters, and interpreters must be placed in the field. It may also indeed require Victim Witness Unit involvement in coordination and security officers. There is no indication -- there is simply no indication that there is any significant financial saving at all, nor is there any particular saving of time. In fact, as we all learned last July, the taking of the deposition is just as intensive as trial. It is a huge effort. It is exactly like being in trial. And if Your Honours will please forgive me - and I mean this only with the greatest respect - the only persons that it saves time for are the three Judges. And again, please, I mean no disrespect by that. But all -- for the attorneys, for the parties, for the court staff, for the reporters, for the interpreters, for everything else, it requires at least the same amount of time. It would be even a greater hardship to do that in Mostar. Also, another concern would be security. Throughout the life of this Tribunal, there have been many times when there have been proposals for the Judges to go to Bosnia in the course of the proceedings, to take a view, or to otherwise carry out or have whole proceedings in Bosnia. I can't say that I can rule out the possibility that's ever -- that that's never happened, but I don't think it has. And if it has happened, it's on a very, very unique and isolated basis. And in fact, again, in this case, in the Chamber's decision on the Defence motion for an on-site visit dated the 5th of October, 2001, this Chamber made the following ruling: "Considering that the Chamber, following consultation with the security section of the Tribunal, is of the opinion that an on-site visit at this stage is not advisable denies the motion." Now, again, presumably, Your Honours, the Judges are not only concerned for their own security and these very same security concerns would apply to the hearing officer, the registry staff, the court reporters, the interpreters, and others. In sum, Mr. President, Your Honours, based on the information provided to date, the Prosecution has no basis to agree to any of the depositions are appropriate. And as we have indicated, we oppose the taking of depositions in Mostar. As to the 92 bis statements, our position is similar. The Prosecution position on that, again as we've stated since last fall, is that we have not been provided to date with sufficient information to make any judgement on the propriety of any evidence being presented by way of Rule 92 bis. First, as with the depositions, Rule 92 bis expressly on its face sets out a number of showings that have to be made and factors to be considered in determining whether evidence is suitable for presentation under Rule 92 bis. None of those showings have been made. Further, no such statements, not even propose -- the proposed 92 bis statements, have been provided to the Prosecution. Indeed, Your Honours, the Prosecution has not been provided to date with a single Defence witness statement of any sort, of any sort, let alone under 92 bis. 92 bis (E) provides: "a party seeking to adduce a written statement or transcript shall give fourteen days notice to the opposing party, who may within seven days object. The Trial Chamber shall decide, after hearing the parties, whether to admit the statement or transcript in whole or in part and whether to require the witness to appear for cross-examination." That means, in our interpretation, that the proposed 92 bis statements themselves must be tendered on at least 14 days notice in order for the Prosecution to review them and express a judgement, or express a view. We have no such statements, Mr. President. We've never even been provided a statement. We have no idea what the proposed 92 bis witness statements would consist of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll discuss specific issues at a later stage. So I believe that this matter will be brought up later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I won't -- that concludes my comments on 92 bis in any event. Turning very quickly, Mr. President, to, as I said, various miscellaneous matters. The defence has raised the question of safe passage. Now, from what's been said today, apparently some motions have been filed. That was the reference that was made. We have seen no such motions. We're not aware of them or the basis for them. So if they're not -- if they're ex parte, and we're not entitled to see them, well, that's one thing. But we're not aware of the motion, so we're not very well in a position to respond to them. However, I can say that we would be surprised by a situation where the Prosecution would be required to give some sort of carte blanche across-the-board safe passage to all defence witnesses whether -- knowing what the situation of any particular witness would be. We're simply not in a position to express any other view on that at this time and have never seen, to our knowledge, such motions. If I'm mistaken on that and they've been mixed in with some other papers received, then I'm sure I'll be corrected. Your Honour, the witness summaries, Mr. Krsnik touched on that, and the Chamber knows from our filings, and it goes back again to what we were just talking about concerning the Rule 71 depositions and the Rule 92 bis statements. We are not satisfied with the witness summaries. They do not provide fair and adequate information. For the most part, they are extremely generic. Many of them are of the nature - and I don't either exaggerate at all, or if I do, by very little - when they say "witness lived in Mostar during the war and will talk about relations between the Croats and Muslims." Well, with all respect, Your Honours, that's not very helpful. And all one has to do by comparison, and we invite the Chamber to do so if you've not done so already, is to take the 65 ter filings that the Prosecution made and put them side by side with the Defence summaries, and the comparison will speak for itself. Mr. Krsnik has indicated issues with translations. We are not unsympathetic. I want to be clear about that, Your Honours. We are not unsympathetic to the issues that translation presents for this institution. All of us know that. You know that. But I must say, we are extremely concerned to hear that 80 per cent of the exhibits are not translated. We have no idea how the Prosecution can possibly receive the Defence witness testimony and possibly prepare for cross-examination without having the documents translated. I think that will rise to a very major issue in a very short time, but I won't belabour it more at the moment. Two final points, or perhaps only one, Mr. President: the Mostar court file. I have told Mr. Krsnik today, and I tell the Chamber the same thing I told him: Ever since he made that request to us, we have made a concerted effort throughout the OTP to find if in fact any such file is in our possession. I can only represent to the Chamber that a number of individuals and a number of person hours have been spent trying to locate or, indeed, identify if we even have such a file. As of this moment, we can locate no such file in the possession of the OTP. I have never seen it, nor have I ever seen any indictment from the Mostar court dealing with alleged crimes in Sovici. We will continue looking, and I can assure the Chamber -- I hope the Chamber realises by now, given our past performance, the past performance of the Prosecution, if we find such a file, it will certainly be turned over. Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I just ask you on that point, are you saying the file has never been in the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We have no -- we have no record of having received that file so far. But again, I'm continuing to look. As the Chamber may know, there is a particular unit called "the rules of the road unit" that receives domestic cases for review. We've checked with the records of that unit. We've also checked with other records to determine if we can find such a file or whether it is recorded anywhere as having come into the OTP. And as of this moment, we can find no such record. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I've got a question to ask you. That is, have you received the Defence counsel's motion as for the taking of depositions which was filed on the 14th of March, 2002, in accordance with Rule 71? I received this motion this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We're expecting the written response from the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Obviously, Your Honours, we'll do that. I think the Chamber can be confident that the written response will track the comments that I made to the Chamber a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now other matters about those court's files. The Defence counsel indicated that those files might involve some exculpatory evidence which is beneficial to the Defence. I just want to remind you that you are under the continued obligation to furnish all those informations about the existence of this evidence. And at the same time, I would like to tell the Defence counsel that if you need any assistance in this respect, we are ready to help you in this respect, upon your request by the form of a motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not intend to speak long, but two brief sentences only. I wish to say only a few words in respect of what the Prosecutor had to say. I really do not know what my learned friend has in mind when he speaks about standards, especially when he speaks about standards of summaries, when that was never adopted. I really don't know what my learned friend, the Prosecutor, means when he invokes the practice of this Court and some kind of extraordinary circumstances. Well, after all this, the Tribunal was founded seven years ago, and it has been functioning for seven years now, and it's not something that is carved in stone. It develops in the interest of justice. And it is true, Your Honours, that we said it is in the interest of justice that all witnesses be heard before the Trial Chamber. That is true. I still assert that. That is why we asked why this Trial Chamber or a delegated judge would not go to Mostar, to one single building of a united court for both the east and west side of Mostar, in the interest of justice. The houses are only 100 metres away. Everybody will be glad to come and say what they have to say. And isn't that in the interest of justice and fairness? Are we really going to be guided by the principle that the Defence has an advantage because some witnesses didn't want to come? Could my learned friend say to me, Your Honours, that the witnesses for the Defence and the witnesses for the Prosecution are the same, that they're in the same position? Well, indirectly, I have been told today - and it's being repeated once again on account of safe passage - that I will need -- well, that they are the ones who are really in charge. Our list of witnesses is well known. Wouldn't it be only fair, professionally fair, to say, "Okay, ask for safe passage for two, three, four, five of these, and it won't be required for the rest?" Are we going to play games as to who is better versed in procedure? And are we going to compete as to who is going to present more truthful evidence here? So that the Trial Chamber could get a full picture of what happened. It's not that Bosnia-Herzegovina parachuted into this world in 1990. Your Honours, indeed, after everything that the Defence went through over the past seven months, we do have reasons to be bitter to a certain extent; however, my professionalism does not allow me to become prey of my motions. Also, when they asked me whether I'm going to call character witnesses, am I going to call character witnesses: If truth and facts will not help me win, why would I need someone who was going to speak nicely about my client? When I came to The Hague, I came with a big heart, an open heart, that this is world justice that is being served here and this is the last chance that my client has to be heard, and everything has to be presented before this Court in the interest of the truth and justice, and that is the only purpose. That is how I experience this, and I see that this Trial Chamber shares the same views. I don't want to go into further comments. I believe that you have understood the core of my response to my learned friend the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, as the matter of the safe passage, I think this Chamber will make the proper decisions in the due time, and it is not the subject of debate at this moment. As for the issue of the deposition, we'll take into the consideration of the views you expressed, and we have plenty of time to debate it later on. But at this moment, it's not the right time for you to argue with the Prosecution. Shall we come to the next issue, specific issue, that is, the 65 ter filings. Well, in the most recent filings, the Defence counsel for Mr. Martinovic proposed the total number of 37 to 40 witnesses, including two expert witnesses. No deposition on Rule 71 witness has been proposed. Generally speaking, I have to say that I'm satisfied with your filings on the list and summary of the testimony of the witnesses. The only problem is the list of the witnesses is a little bit too long, as you explained to us just now. In accordance with Rule 73 ter, this Trial Chamber could set the number of the witnesses and shorten the estimated length of the examination-in-chief of some witnesses, whatever is shorter. Taking into consideration of the 57 witnesses in 69 days by the -- in the Prosecution's case, in my personal view, 25 to 30 witnesses heard in the court will be a reasonable number. So Mr. Krsnik, would you please consider restructuring your witness list by dividing them as witnesses in principal and witnesses in reserve so that you may make the best use of the Rule 71 of deposition as well as 92 bis for some witnesses in reserve. This is just a suggestion, not an order. Could I get a response from Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Vinko Martinovic has always abided by your decisions and shall continue to do so in the future as well; however, in relation to the number of witnesses, at first we had 120, and then we further eliminated some witnesses, and then we had about 85, and we informed the Trial Chamber thereof. With the best of will, with the best of intentions to make the proceedings as efficacious as possible, I think that this number of witnesses is an optimum number in order to truly bring these proceedings to a close properly, not only in the views -- in the view of the Defence but we also believe that in this way, the Trial Chamber will have obtained a complete picture with regard to my client. These witnesses are not repetitious. These witnesses are testifying with regard to different circumstances that are very important for our defence case. However - however - perhaps we can find a way to do something with a few of them, that is to say, as we proceed, perhaps we could bring the number down further. But Your Honours, in view of the timetable envisaged, I think that we really are keeping abreast of what you have asked for. We have already proven this through our submissions. We do not have any proposal for depositions. I already said that. Of course, I don't want to enter a debate with my learned friend the Prosecutor now, but I am so sorry that he is holding our arguments against Mr. Naletilic's defence. We are not in the same position. Item number 3 of this agenda, we have no written statements. I mean, I am moving further down the agenda, expert witnesses. Could I perhaps speak again, or should I speak about it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, later on, you'll have another chance. And I appreciate that your statement, by saying that you'll do something with few of your witnesses later on. We appreciate that. As for the 65 ter filings filed by the Defence counsel of Naletilic, I must confess that we have big problems with these filings. During the Status Conference, this Trial Chamber mentioned three criteria for the testimony of witnesses provided by the Defence which should be served as kind of guidance. The first one, I remembered that it is very clear that the Defence counsel do not have to prove your client is innocent but you have to attack the evidence presented by the Prosecution in its case. If the evidence presented by the Prosecutor is not challenged, we probably will believe the matter is not at issue. The second matter is the political debate is not allowed in this trial. We may hear some testimonies on the background, but is it really necessary for us to hear 14 trial witnesses testify on that issue? Some of the repetitive witnesses could be heard through the deposition procedure. The purpose of this Tribunal is to address the personal criminal responsibility rather than the political issues in that area. Thirdly, tu quoque defence is not acceptable in this trial. But there are still some witnesses only testified on this issue, judging from the summary you provided to us. Well, unless you satisfy those standards set by this Trial Chamber, it is very difficult for us to hear those witnesses. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have come to the crucial issue, as far as the Defence is concerned. We, the Defence, have been thinking about this since the day we entered this courtroom. We have been doing our best to adjust to the standards adopted here in terms of time and the number of witnesses concerned, on the one hand, and on the other hand, what we have to refute, that which has to be presented here as the truth. Not a single one of my witnesses is being called for political purposes or to illustrate the political situation. These are participants in concrete events, and they are concretely challenging and denying the charges made in the indictment. For example, Witness number 1, who is a member of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could we please move into private session, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my -- I apologise. My client has been charged with all the counts in the indictment, and I have to challenge each count. It is nice to hear that the Defence does not have to prove innocence, but we are forced to do this. It is up to us. These witnesses should have been brought here by the OTP seven years ago. The legal tradition I have been raised in tells me so; however, the proceedings here are quite different from the proceedings in our countries. Why do I have to bring some witnesses in? Because the OTP never interviewed them, never bothered to look for them, never bothered to bring them here. So it's up to the Defence. It's up to us, of course, to challenge the evidence adduced here. And believe me, Your Honour, this is the minimum number of witnesses. We can, of course, still alter the number. And of course, we do have to count on acts of God, because we do not know what time will bring. The newspapers will start writing about this. There is a whole machinery, a whole hidden machinery, operating in the background. These witnesses will not testify about politics but about facts, about 80 per cent of the counts in the indictment, the villages of Sovici. Everything else relates to general circumstances. I wanted these witnesses to cover everything, both the facts and the general background. Witness number 3, if you have him here, I think can cover everything: the facts, the circumstances, documents he signed, and so on and so forth. I have tried, Your Honour, to make the issues clear to you, and I hope that you will grant my request, and I will always consult Mr. Fourmy if there are any changes that need to be made, with your leave, any alterations in the number of witnesses and so on, because the witnesses are on their way already. Some of them are already on their way. They're arriving tomorrow. It's very hard for me now to change anything. But I will not keep you any longer. I do hope you have understood my submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we have already gone through all those, you know, lists of the witness. At least judging from the summaries you submitted, some of them will get us nowhere. We don't want you to present your case at this moment to the Prosecution, but there have to be some indications about the charges in the indictment. To be a live witness, except those background witnesses, what we want to hear is his personal knowledge of the involvement of your client in the certain incidents charged in the indictment. We believe that's the most important things for the defence of your case. It seems to me during the two submissions - one is the 65 ter, and another is the Rule 71 - you somehow got confused with each other. We believe that some witnesses listed as the deposition witnesses should be heard as a trial witness and some witnesses listed in the 65 ter list should be deposition witnesses. And we'll discuss it when we come to the next item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It's not really a question, Mr. Krsnik. It's just that I don't want you to think for a moment that we don't appreciate how difficult it is to be Defence counsel and what a huge burden all of you carry in a war crimes Tribunal case. But we just want to, without being in any way offensive and without having you think that we don't recognise the enormous efforts that you have gone to, to collate a list of very important witnesses. We want to sort of direct you towards the specific charges within the background as your client perceives it because obviously there's another side to the story. We recognise that totally. But what we're concerned about -- and as I said, this is not really a question. What we're concerned about is that so much time is being spent presenting the other side of a political argument which we recognise already. We recognise from the questions you've raised and from the many documents we've read that obviously there were issues in the early days of the setting up of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and the recognition of the HVO as being the authority, the setting up of a civil service. We're aware of that background and the umbrella of legality or apparent legality at the time. But what we're concerned about is that you should direct your energies and your skills towards responding to the specific allegations that have been made by the witnesses for the Prosecution and where we have already decided that you have a case to meet. In other words, that if we accept what those witnesses say, then your client is in trouble, if we say that. Now, it's up to you through your witnesses to dispute that evidence. And that's what we'd like you to Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 8761 to 8766 direct your main energies towards. So if we were to hear two or three or four of your very best witnesses, the most articulate, the most educated, in relation to the early days, the background, and obviously we can see what direction you're going in, the reasons why so many Muslims were detained at the beginning of conflict and during the conflict. If you then direct your arguments to what your client has to meet, that he's guilty of persecution -- sorry, that's the allegation that's made, that he's guilty of persecution, of torture, of inhumane treatment. And that's -- so direct your energies because your witness summaries don't seem to give the impression to us at the moment that you're focussed enough on that. Do you understand what we're saying? It's not a criticism. We're trying to assist you, and we're also not being patronising, either. I hope you realise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As always, you are directing me in the right direction. Maybe it's because the summaries have not been properly compiled. We are directing our energies at disputing what is being charged against my client, and we are doing so through these witnesses. I can now say that when the highest representatives of the then-government testify, they will not know who my client was, or rather, they will not know him personally. But when -- we will bring other witnesses who will testify that it could not have been him. So we have paid special attention to this. And all our witnesses will testify precisely to what Your Honour has said. It is possible that because I am so exhausted because I have been working so hard, up to 20 hours a day, that I may have confused some things. Some witnesses may be more important than others. But I tried to have witnesses who can cover many issues, not just one or two, so that we can make the best possible use of them, while witnesses who -- for example, a witness testifying about prisoners in Siroki Brijeg, these are witnesses who will testify only for about 20 minutes, not for long, and their testimonies will be very clear and short. They will say, "Yes, I was the person who was there," and so on and so forth, and then I will hand them over to the Prosecution for cross-examination. I will not waste time with these witnesses. These witnesses we would like to testify through depositions, because then we can go through 20 witnesses in a very short time. But I do agree with your suggestion, and I accept it, and I understand, I allow for the fact that I may have confused some issues. Now I understand and I will make some changes. I would need a break after the first few witnesses so that I can change the order, because now arrangements have already been made for the witnesses to come here. I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Seric. But I've been asked to have a break, you know. If you will be very concise, I'll let you go. Yes, please, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, very briefly. To avoid giving the impression that the Defence of Vinko Martinovic is pretending that we have nothing to do with witnesses that Mr. Krsnik intends to call to begin with, they are common witnesses, and we support the comments made by Mr. Krsnik. That's all I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, I'm afraid we have to take a break at this moment. We will resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we start, I was reminded that the third criteria for the Defence - I mentioned it just now - was not in the transcript. I want to repeat that the Defence of the tu quoque is not acceptable in this trial, just for the sake of the record. The next issue is about the deposition, Rule 71. I believe that this issue has been debated already. And there's just one point I want to mention concerned with this matter, that is this Trial Chamber is seized with a motion filed by Defence counsel of Mr. Naletilic dated 14th of March, 2002, to take deposition for use at the trial per Rule 71. And as I mentioned before, that we are expecting the response from the Prosecution side. I would like to make an initial response for the remarks made by Mr. Krsnik just now. And I think we agree with you that the deposition procedure will be judicially economic and will streamline the actual trial. And in the interests of justice, your client is entitled to have a fair and expeditious trial. At this moment, I would like to remind the parties of a decision made by this Trial Chamber, with different composition, on November 10th, 2000, on the Prosecutor's motion to take deposition for use at trial. The Trial Chamber highlighted that the witnesses proposed for depositions will not present eyewitness evidence directly implicating the accused in the crimes charged, or alternatively, their evidence will be of repetitive nature in the sense that many witnesses will give evidence of similar facts. In light of this decision, we believe that some witnesses proposed for deposition should be trial witnesses, since they have the firsthand knowledge of the accused's involvement in the crime charged, and some of the trial witnesses should be deposition witnesses, since their testimony has nothing to do with the accused and is repetitive. In this sense, we hope that the Defence could restructure the witnesses in both categories. Are there anything more to say on this subject? Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Not from the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we come to the next item. That is the written statement submitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the Rules. Mr. Scott already mentioned his positions and his points of view just now. We want to hear the response from Defence counsel on this issue. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We shall certainly abide by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and we shall disclose this 14 days before the witness is brought in. But we have problems with the translation. We have identified priorities and have drawn up a list of priorities for translation so that, I hope that with the assistance of the Registry and all concerned, we shall succeed in this. We shall certainly take care that any evidence we wish to present is disclosed 14 days in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We're satisfied with your response and will instruct the registrar to do their utmost to have those statements translated. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. My colleague has drawn my attention to five statements, or rather, a total of seven which are being translated in the field and which will be certified by a court in the field. And these shall be delivered to the Prosecution on time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Krsnik, this doesn't really arise out of what we were saying just now, but I had been thinking about it. And what you told us about these parallel indictments, how did you come by this information and, you know, when did you come by the information? It's disturbing me a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be pleased to answer your question, Your Honour. Working with witnesses in the field in early March, that is, some two weeks ago, a witness I was working with brought me an indictment he had obtained, or rather, it was his indictment. It was an indictment that he obtained through the Ministry of Justice of the federation. And his name is mentioned on the indictment. He showed it to me, and this was a shock for me. So I set out to investigate. The other witness who has been indicted and is charged with crimes connected to camps, I would like us to go into private session so I can tell you the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber wishes to inform the parties that it would like to deal with the issue of protective measures in the same way as it did for the Prosecution witnesses. Having noticed that the Defence of Naletilic already indicated for most of the witnesses what protective measures they will request, nevertheless the Chamber would like to remind the parties that they should indicate as early as possible which protective measures their witnesses wish to have. If a witness requests closed session, an application should be made in writing in advance. Requests for pseudonym and facial distortion may be made orally before the respective witness testifies. With regard to voice distortion, request must be made in advance, as the technical person will need some time to organise the requested equipment. However, again, such application may be made either orally or in writing. We understand that there are some witnesses in the first ten witnesses list will request the closed session. So we'll ask Defence counsel to submit a motion for that, because we believe that, in principle, all the hearings in this Tribunal should be public. Are there anything to say by both parties on this very issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krznic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. The next issue is exhibits. In our decisions on the pre-Defence filings, the parties were asked to provide a list of their exhibits and to coordinate with the registrar in relation to the pre-numbering issues. I would like to draw the attention of both parties to the fact that the registrar has already furnished us with a binder of the documents concerned with the numbering of the exhibits, as well as the numbering of the witnesses. We hope that the registrar will get into consultations with the Defence in organising all those exhibits as well as to explain how to use the numbering system. Yes. Could I turn to the registrar, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to draw everyone's attention that the bundle that I prepared for the parties today has instructions and some general information that will help aid the Defence counsel in preparing their case. I also attached the minutes from the trial management meeting that was held on September 7th, 2001, which also will give the Defence a chance to review some of the necessary things needed. And also, I prepared the completed Prosecution's exhibit list. I'm meeting with the Defence again after this hearing to finalise their exhibit list and how we're going to work that out, and that will be provided to the Chamber, to the senior legal officer, and to the OTP as soon as that is completed. I also supplied them with the numbering of how the pseudonyms will be and the witness sheet will be labelled. So we've covered just about everything that you requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam. Any comments on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution may have a couple of more or less closing comments, if you will. One would touch on the exhibits. But I can either make that particular comment now or I would have a couple of comments that I would like to address to the Chamber at the end, and I'm in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if it's related to the exhibits, you may address this issue. And we also have the last item is for the other issues, miscellaneous matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Your Honour, the point is this, and it is -- relates to the miscellaneous issues as well. As we indicated earlier, we are very concerned, the Prosecution is very concerned, of course, about the handling of the exhibits and translations of these items. The Chamber's ruling on the 12th of March indicated that the exhibit list would be filed -- an additional list of exhibits or indeed a list of exhibits would be filed today. Of course, we have not yet seen that. So we're very anxious to see -- have that filing, Your Honour, as well as the additional filing which the Chamber ordered in the same order for the additional information about witnesses. I'll leave that for now, Your Honour. I'll leave my other remarks for a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could I hear the response from Defence counsel. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have today filed our list of exhibits, and I believe that the Prosecution will have this by the end of the day or by tomorrow. We have abided by all your decisions, and we have put on the list all of those that have been translated. And as the translations come in, we are going to add these exhibits to the list, because we have no reason not to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We appreciate that. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say the following in relation to the Martinovic defence and the documents. We have presented our standpoint, which is quite similar. We have no documents. We are going to use the documents that were used by the Prosecution. The only documents that we have is the expert opinion of Dr. Skaric that has been provided already in this case, and we have also announced that we would perhaps carry out expertise of a particular Prosecution witness. We haven't had appropriate documents yet that would lend itself to expertise. In the meantime, we have received these documents, and we have submitted this to the OTP and to the Trial Chamber. If we come into possession of other documents that we might use during our Defence case, we are going to provide them in timely fashion to the Prosecution. This is our standpoint with regard to documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just an additional bit of information. We also have a CD with maps. Different situations are depicted in them: military situations, camps, refugee flows, et cetera. There is a large number of them. We have had these CDs burned, to put it in poplar terms, and these copies are being made. We will let the OTP have copies as soon as possible. However, we have a problem with the video. We agreed today that we can submit this videotape, although it hasn't been translated yet. I'll have to work in concert with the video unit. And I would like to say at this point in time that we will do our best to provide our colleagues from the OTP with this in a timely manner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Just one point in relation to the exhibits that this Defence team is compiling. We just have one request. I already mentioned this during the Prosecution case. We have submitted this request to the office of the president of the republic, and we were told that we should approach the office for cooperation with the ICTY. We are seeking a presidential transcript, especially after your ruling deciding on this, and we have not received an answer until the present day. So this is the particular exhibit that we are awaiting. If we do not receive this soon, Your Honours, we shall address you yet again to seek your assistance so that we could obtain this from the Croatian government, the Croatian state. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me give the floor to Mr. Scott first. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one comment and request to the Chamber. I heard primarily Mr. Krsnik say a moment ago -- and perhaps it applies to both Defence teams -- that documents would be added to the exhibit list as documents were translated. Now, I have two comments on that. That sounds to me like it's a moving exhibit list which will be changed more or less at random, so we have no idea what the exhibit list will look like ten days from now or three weeks from now because apparently it will change over time. That's one concern. The second concern is this: We would be anxious to have -- and we only think it would be fair, even if the B/C/S documents can be provided to us. It will come as no surprise and no secret that the OTP does have a number of people on its staff who work and read in B/C/S. So even if they're not translated, if the counsel could be so kind as to provide us with those documents in a timely fashion so that we could prepare for them, we can have people look at them, short of being -- short of the translations coming in. So if I can be clear on that, Your Honours, I don't think it's fair to the Prosecution for B/C/S documents to be held back and not disclosed pending translation, when we'd be most anxious to receive the B/C/S documents as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, is what you're saying if I understand you right, is that even if a document is not translated, that is no reason for its identity not to be clearly specified on the list? In other words, just because a document is awaiting translation doesn't mean that it doesn't appear on the list. Every document appears on the list. The translation comes later. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That exactly would be our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that seems a very fair position to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe there is a misunderstanding. The Defence did not say that they would be changing the list or adjusting the list. We are just tackling things in order. As exhibits are translated, we are going to submit them. As for the list of exhibits that have not been translated yet, we haven't made a list of this nature. In addition to that, you may remember, Your Honours, how much we listened to our friend Mr. Scott with regard to the disclosure of documents, that they are not duty-bound, that we are not duty-bound, et cetera, et cetera. The Defence is not going to act that way. If the gentleman would like to see the documents in the Croatian language, we would only be too happy to provide them to him. You will see, Your Honours, all the time we will be behaving in such a way as to show that we are interested in nothing but bringing this case to a close, to have everything heard that should be heard, and that is the truth, namely, your ruling, and we are not interested in anything else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that point, that requires a response. That kind of a speech requires a very short response. Mr. Krsnik says he's interested in nothing but justice. The Prosecution has not received a single piece of disclosure at this point, not a single witness statement, not a single exhibit. The Defence case starts on Monday. And for counsel to stand up and say that he's only interested in justice and everything coming out is inappropriate and contrary to the way that the Defence is being conducted. And I apologise for that comment, Your Honour, but I believe the response was necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, if you're reading the decisions on the pre-Defence findings by this Trial Chamber, it says clearly that the Defence counsel shall disclose the list of the exhibits, rather than the documents themselves. They are under no obligation to disclose all those materials they are going to use in their case. I think we should make a very clear distinction between the two issues. Another matter is there may be some more documents in the process of the Defence case, and the list should be allowed to be amended and to be added with more documents. But another matter I want to say is that which is mainly directed to the Defence counsel of Martinovic. If you are using the 17 binders of those documents, and before you present your case, you have to inform the Chamber, the registrar, and the other party which particular documents you are going to use at least one day before that. We cannot bring all those 17 binders of documents in court. Yes, Mr. Par. Do you want to make a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish to confirm that this is precisely the way in which we intend to use the documents. We will work in the same way as the Prosecutor has. We shall do exactly what you have said, and there will be no problems on our side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Shall we turn to the next issue? That is the procedural matters of the Defence case. There's two questions we want to ask to the Defence counsel. As Mr. Krsnik mentioned, that he will deliver opening statements before his case. We wonder whether the Defence counsel for Mr. Martinovic will also make an opening statement and when will that opening statement will be delivered. Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the defence of Vinko Martinovic will give an opening statement but not on Monday. We shall deliver it on a day to be determined by the Trial Chamber before we begin the presentation of our case and the examination of our witnesses, that is, at the beginning of our part of the defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for that. Another matter is: Do the accused themselves wish to make a unsworn statement in line with Rule 84 bis? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. They will not avail themselves of this right, as they stated at the beginning of this trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at present, we shall not avail ourselves of this right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [Trial Chamber confers]. If later on you change your mind on this very issue, please inform the Trial Chamber of this matter. Well, the last issue is dealing with other issues, that is, miscellaneous matters. Mr. Scott, just now you mentioned that you have something to say on this subject. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In the course of the last few comments, admittedly most of them have been said. But a couple of things. Let me come back for a moment, because there was a certain -- there was an exchange between counsel and the Court and one item might have been clarified but there was a second item which the Prosecution also is quite concerned about. Mr. Krsnik has represented, and I believe his representation or take it to be true that the witness list or some witness list has been filed today, that it apparently hasn't made its way to us yet. There was a second part, as the Chamber will know, of the 12th of March order, that ordered "that the Defence file additional information about the witnesses they intend to call," and that was also due. It was to be filed prior to the pre-Defence conference on the 20th of March, 2002. So I'm also concerned whether that additional submission has been made. And while I raise that, Your Honour, to finish up and make the comments that I told the Chamber I would request to make, Your Honour, we continue to be very concerned that the various Defence filings - and I want the record to be clear on this - that the various Defence filings are inadequate to the Prosecution to reasonably prepare to meet the Defence cases. We have stated that in our various filings, and we want to reaffirm that at this point. I want to make a couple of examples, simply, and I will do it very quickly. But in the supplemental Defence filings for the accused Naletilic filed on the 15th of March, 2002 -- and we're not going to mention names, so I don't think private session is necessary. But on page 11, Witness J, this is the summary that's been provided to the Prosecution. Well, Your Honour, out of an abundance of caution, we'll go to private session just to avoid the possibility that someone will say that someone might be identified. The Chamber will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I already have that, you know, documents at my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You don't have to quote the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Your Honour. Of course you're right. I will just simply, for example, refer the Chamber to Witness J, the summary, which is literally one sentence. I refer to Witness AB on page 17, which is two sentences. I refer the Chamber to Witness AG, which is on page 18, which is literally one sentence of the most generic character. Now, on top of that, unlike the situation with the Defence, when we filed our 65 ter filings twice, first in 2000, a year before the trial started, and again shortly before trial, not only did they have the summaries, they had the witness statements. Mr. President, this is all we have. We have no witness statements. We have in some instances two sentences or one sentence of the most generic possible character. We object to that. We want to state our objection. We do not believe that that's fair that they're -- just as the Defence has rights, the Prosecution has rights, as was recognised by the Chamber in the Aleksovski case in its decision in February of 1999. The Prosecutor acts on behalf of the international community, including the victims. The victims are entitled to a fair trial. The international community is entitled to a fair trial. And the filings that have been made by the Defence, particularly the Naletilic Defence, are not adequate and it is not fair to the Prosecutor or to the international community or to the victims. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. You have to be very concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. The Defence of Mladen Naletilic respects the international community and is now standing before a Tribunal set up by the international community. The Defence of Mladen Naletilic has not taken any witness statements. All we have are our notes. The Prosecutor, Your Honour, seems not to understand the roles, who is prosecuting and who is defending here. We have the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the Statute of this Tribunal. But today at our meeting, I asked Mr. Scott personally something that had to do with the objection he has just raised. I said to him, "Which statements do you want us to expand, and we shall do it." And he didn't give me a reply at our meeting. But now he keeps talking about the international community and a fair trial. Maybe, just as I became confused about the witnesses -- I don't want to insult anyone because I deeply respect my learned friend but he seems to have confused the roles of Prosecutor and Defence counsel. If I have no statement, I cannot provide one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let me make some comments on the -- Mr. Scott's statement. First of all, this Trial Chamber does not believe that Defence counsel has any obligation to provide to the Prosecution with the previous statement of potential witnesses. Secondly, as for the specific informations or summaries in the 65 ter filings made by the Defence counsel, we agree with the comments Mr. Scott made just now. We are not satisfied, as I mentioned before, with those summaries. And we have already mentioned that when we came across this issue earlier. That's why we made the decisions on the 12th of March, requesting the Defence counsel to furnish additional information or indications of the witnesses' testimony so that we could have some guidance as to the testimony of that witness. I believe Mr. Krsnik will do that, as required by this Trial Chamber. Another matter is that just now we have already mentioned, that the Trial Chamber was seized of a request of the order of disclosure by the Prosecution filed by the Defence of Naletilic on March 8th, 2002, in which it was submitted that the Prosecution was in possession of exculpatory evidence from the high court in Mostar. We would like to know whether the Prosecution would like to respond to this request or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, do you want me to respond to it -- do you mean now, or would you like a written response? I believe this is the matter that's already been addressed earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sure. We hope that it will be in the form of a written response.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any matters that both parties would like to raise at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one matter. When can we have you know ex parte session, the one -- the hearing that the Defence requested, because this is a very important question and we also want to discuss the disclosure of witnesses for whom we have asked for special protective measures, and we would like to get your decision on this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll bring this matter with the other members of this Bench and set a date as well as soon as possible, with the consultations of the registrar. This is all I could do in response to your question. So having said that, I believe that's all for this pre-Defence conference. We will rise and we'll see you next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 5.15 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of March, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
